newsitem.title: UK: North Sea, Nigerian crudes buoyed by arbitrage.
newsitem.headline: North Sea, Nigerian crudes buoyed by arbitrage.

text.p: North Sea and West African crude continued to benefit from strong U.S. and east Asian demand, but buyers held back on Thursday after a two-day buying spree.
Traders said most wet crude differentials maintained their recent strength despite a falling Brent futures market.
IPE February Brent oscillated between $23.62 and $24.00 per barrel over the day, and by 1815 GMT stood at $23.75 per barrel, 17 cents below Wednesday's close.
A 3-day delay in Statfjord loadings kept some heat under the market and with low inventories at refineries, one trader said this might bring out a few last-minute buyers.
Loadings in December and January were pushed back due to problems restarting production after maintenance at the Statfjord B platform earlier this week, traders said.

A cargo of Dated Brent loading on December 28-30 traded at Jan -20 cents, 1.5 cents below Wednesday's price. "That was the last cargo of the month -- a bit of a one-off. We are seeing good demand in the first decade of January and the U.S. arb is wide open," a North Sea equity holder said.
In the past eight days, the Dated Brent/LLS spread has grown by $1.80 to $3.00 per barrel.
Of the two Brent dates to be nominated into the paper chain on Thursday, one was kept by Stasco and the other clocked to J Aron, dealers said.
Forties crude continued to trade on a confidential basis, with the bid/ask spread at Dated Brent +27/35 cents.

West African crude was propped up by heavy Korean and Chinese demand, on top of steady U.S. and European buying. A January 10-20 Forcados traded earlier this week at Dated Brent +75 cents, and Bonny Light was valued at Dated +65 cents.
NNPC kept customers waiting for the January contract prices, which one contract holder expected to rise by five cents.
